sum: Airbus put capital returns and commercial demand at the center of investor attention during the week of November 9-13, 2026. The company launched a multi-year share buyback on November 9 and announced a new Cathay aircraft order on November 11.

Airbus said on November 9 that the programme could run through July 31, 2029 and reach up to 5 billion euros. The first tranche runs from November 9 through December 23 and is capped at 800 million euros, subject to market conditions. Airbus said it intends to cancel the shares it acquires.

The programme gives Airbus an additional way to return capital while the company manages aircraft production, deliveries and cash conversion. For investors, execution pace and the eventual share count reduction are the next practical points to monitor.
Airbus said the buyback is subject to continued shareholder approval and applicable market-abuse rules.
On November 11, Cathay Group placed a firm order for 14 additional Airbus aircraft, according to the Airbus press release. The order comprises 11 A330-900s and three A321neos.

The deal lifts Cathay Group's firm commitment for the A330-900 to 41 aircraft. Airbus said the aircraft will support Cathay's regional and longer-haul operations, while the A330-900 deliveries are scheduled to build on the airline's fleet renewal and expansion plans.

For Airbus, the order reinforces widebody and single-aisle demand, although the financial effect will depend on production timing, delivery execution and the conversion of orders into revenue and cash flow.

Airbus stock in focus after Cathay orders 14 jets
sum: Airbus said on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, that Hong Kong's Cathay Group had placed a firm order for 14 additional aircraft. The order comprises 11 A330-900 widebody jets and three A321neos, according to the Airbus press release.

The announcement strengthens Airbus's commercial aircraft backlog and gives the manufacturer another fleet-renewal commitment from a major Asian airline group. Cathay said the A330-900s will support Cathay Pacific's regional network, adding passenger and cargo capacity, while the A321neos will support the growth of its low-cost subsidiary HK Express on mainland China and other short-haul routes.

The additional A330-900s build on Cathay's 2024 order for 30 aircraft. The new commitment lifts the group's firm order total for the type to 41. The three A321neos add to a previous 2023 order for 32 A321neo and A320neo aircraft.

For Airbus, the mix provides exposure to two parts of Cathay's network plan. The A330-900 addresses regional and potentially longer flights, while the A321neo offers capacity for shorter routes. Airbus said the two aircraft families give Cathay flexibility to match capacity with demand and benefit from a streamlined Airbus fleet.

Cathay Chief Operations and Service Delivery Officer Alex McGowan said the order would help expand and upgrade the fleet, support regional operations across Asia-Pacific and provide greater flexibility on longer flights. Airbus Commercial Aircraft sales executive Benoit de Saint-Exupery described the order as an endorsement of the aircraft families' role in Cathay's growth.

The Airbus release did not disclose the purchase price or an individual delivery schedule. It said the A330neo is powered by Rolls-Royce Trent 7000 engines and is designed for a range of up to 8,100 nautical miles. Those product claims describe the aircraft's technical positioning; they do not establish the financial contribution of this order to Airbus.

Airbus stock traded at 208.93 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 11:06 CET on Wednesday, November 11. Investors will continue to weigh new order intake against delivery execution, production rates and cash generation as Airbus works through its commercial aircraft expansion plans.

sum: Airbus delivered its 700th aircraft to the Lufthansa Group, handing over the airline's first A350-1000 in the same transaction. The twin landmark ties a long-running delivery relationship to the carrier's introduction of a new widebody type.
The handover caps a busy stretch for the European planemaker, which is simultaneously pressing toward its full-year delivery target, buying back stock and adding to its defence and space order book.

Between January and October 2026, Airbus handed over 621 aircraft. Management is holding to a full-year goal of 870 planes, which by Reuters calculations leaves roughly 249 deliveries to complete before the calendar runs out. October alone accounted for 74 handovers.

The company's multi-year share repurchase programme, worth up to EUR 5 billion, runs until 31 July 2029, with the acquired shares earmarked for cancellation. A first tranche of up to EUR 800 million opened on the same day as the Lufthansa handover and closes on 23 December 2026.

sum: Airbus handed over 74 aircraft to 45 customers in October, lifting its ten-month delivery total to 621 jets, the European planemaker said. Gross orders for the month reached 202, bringing the year-to-date gross order intake to 1,376. The two figures measure different things: bookings count gross orders placed, while deliveries track aircraft already handed to customers.

The operational update lands alongside the financial framework Airbus published on 28 October, covering the first nine months of 2026. Revenue came in at EUR 50.6 billion, with net profit of EUR 3.59 billion.

On the military side, France's procurement agency DGA qualified the vertical take-off and landing version of Airbus Helicopters' U010 Aliaca drone on Tuesday, clearing the way for its deployment under the French Navy's SMDM contract. Airbus said the first two systems had already been delivered to the Navy in September.
Space work also moved forward. On 27 October Airbus won an order to build two more second-generation Galileo satellites, adding to an existing booking for six.

The same day brought commitments from two aviation customers. Atlantic Airways placed a firm order for two A320neo jets, while Boston MedFlight signed for three H145 helicopters — taking its total H145 purchases to twelve, according to Airbus.
A day earlier, on 26 October, Life Flight Network ordered five H135 helicopters.

Airbus and India's Blue Angels Air signed an agreement on pilot training, with Blue Angels Air set to handle ab initio instruction within the Airbus Flight Academy network. The first cadets are due to begin training in Tunisia in 2027, Airbus said, and the arrangement is aimed squarely at the Indian market.

Airbus Balances Drone Qualification and Digital Services Push Against a Demanding Year-End Delivery
sum: Airbus shares climbed 4.0% on Wednesday in a firm European market, extending a recovery that has been underway since the company reported nine-month results. No fresh corporate announcement drove the move. Instead, investors took their cue from UBS, which kept its "Buy" rating on the stock while trimming its price target to EUR 230 from EUR 240.

The combination matters more than the target cut on its own. A buy recommendation does not mean the Swiss bank expects positive surprises across every horizon. Analyst Ian Douglas-Pennant draws a deliberately time-sensitive picture: Airbus could beat expectations in 2026, he believes, while a result slightly below market consensus is possible in 2027. Near-term strength therefore comes with a caveat for the following year — a distinction that limits how much the day's rally can be read as a vote of confidence in the longer outlook.

Away from the share price, Airbus has been logging progress on several regulatory and service fronts. France's defence procurement agency has qualified the VTOL variant of the U010 Aliaca, the company's vertical take-off and landing tactical unmanned aerial system, following tests conducted in May and June 2026. The decision, reported a day earlier, covers a completed qualification step for that specific variant, developed by Airbus Helicopters.

In Japan, the civil aviation authority granted Airbus Helicopters approval as a development organisation, authorising development work across its helicopter fleet in the country. That announcement was published on 28 October — the same day the company confirmed a 50/50 joint venture with Air France-KLM called Alpha Component Solutions, which will provide worldwide component support for the A350.

Digital services are expanding in parallel. On Monday, Skywise unveiled additional training solutions: the MATe Suite, the Virtual Procedure Trainer and Flight eLearning. These operational developments sit alongside the quarterly figures but are separate from the question of whether Airbus will hit its full-year financial targets.
That question remains the operative benchmark. In the third quarter of 2026, revenue fell 2% year on year to EUR 17.469 billion, while adjusted operating profit dropped 9% to EUR 1.768 billion.

items.t: JetBlue Soars 11%, United Rallies 6% as Oil Drops on Iran Peace Talk Hopes; American Airlines Gains 5%
sum: Oil is tumbling on U.S.-Iran peace talk hopes, and airline stocks are surging in response, but the carrier with the most to gain is also the one with the least room for error if diplomacy falls apart.

Airline stocks are rising as oil prices tumble on hopes that U.S.-Iran talks could ease supply fears, according to reports from The Wall Street Journal, CNBC and the Financial Times. JetBlue Airways (NASDAQ:JBLU) stock is at $3.18, up 11%, early in the session. Even after that jump, JetBlue stock is still down 30% year to date (YTD).

Jet fuel is one of the biggest costs any airline carries, so lower oil prices can quickly improve the profit outlook. JetBlue is the smallest of the five carriers. It is also the most fuel-sensitive in this group, and its shares are posting the largest gain in the group today.

WTI crude oil trades at $97.05 per barrel, down nearly 7% over the past 24 hours, on hopes for U.S.-Iran diplomacy. It comes after oil settled at $109.72 on October 23, so the move marks a retreat from multi-month highs. For JetBlue, the relief hits its most damaging cost.

JetBlue disclosed on October 26 that its Q3 2026 fuel costs surged 61% year over year (YoY) to $868 million at $3.91 per gallon. On an adjusted basis, the company lost $0.60 per share, missing the $0.55 consensus. Looking ahead, the company’s Q4 2026 guidance assumes fuel at $4.64 per gallon, so any lasting drop in oil could feed straight into its earnings.
United Airlines and American Airlines Ride the Same Fuel Relief

United Airlines Holdings (NASDAQ:UAL | UAL Price Prediction) stock is at $110.81, up 6%. Fourth-quarter guidance from United calls for adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of $0.50 to $1.50, based on an average fuel price of $4.80 per gallon. CEO Scott Kirby addressed the 2027 margin goal. He linked it to factors outside the company’s control on the October 21 earnings call: “To get there in 2027, we probably also need at least one of the following three things to happen: lower fuel, lower industry capacity, or a continued willingness for the industry to trade load factor for yield.”

Airbus shares jump on €5 billion buyback, new guidance
sum: July 22 (Reuters) – Airbus shares jumped more than 5% on Wednesday after the European planemaker launched a €5 billion ($5.7 billion) share buyback programme and unveiled new mid-term targets including a near doubling of profits by 2029.

Airbus said late on Tuesday it was targeting a core profit of €12 billion to €13 billion in 2029, which would mark a sharp rise from €7.13 billion of adjusted earnings before interest and taxes last year and is well above the 2026 target of €7.5 billion.
“The positive surprise, however, came from the €5 (billion) three-year share buy-back,” Deutsche Bank analyst Christophe Menard said in a note to investors.

The world’s largest civil planemaker also expects its dominant commercial aircraft business to generate around €10 billion in operating profit in 2029 and struck a positive tone on aircraft deliveries.
Airbus started the year slowly due to supply-chain and engine bottlenecks but has since accelerated deliveries, increasing first-half handovers by 15% year-on-year.
J.P. Morgan wrote that Airbus “delivered on all the things we felt were needed for the shares to rally”.

sum: Aequs shares rose more than 5 percent on Tuesday after Nuvama Institutional Equities initiated coverage on the stock with a 'Buy' rating and a 12-month target price of Rs 444 per share, implying an upside of over 91 percent from the previous session's closing price.

The stock settled at Rs 244.11 pe share on the NSE, up 5.27 percent. During the session, it climbed as much as 6.37 percent to an intraday high of Rs 246.66 after opening with a gap-up of 2.63 percent.

Aequs also emerged as the top gainer in the Nifty India Defence index, which ended 1.65 percent lower. It was among only three stocks in the index to close in the green, along with Zen Technologies and Dynamatic Technologies. The remaining constituents in the defence index ended lower.

Initiating coverage on the company, Nuvama said Aequs is India's only vertically integrated aerospace Special Economic Zone (SEZ) supplying machined aerostructures, landing gear and engine parts to original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) such as Airbus and Boeing.

The brokerage described Aequs as India's first pure-play aerospace precision manufacturer and said its order book of about Rs 7,600 crore provides visibility for a 42 percent sales CAGR and 84 percent EBITDA CAGR during FY26-FY29.
It said the company's manufacturing ecosystem covers machining, forging, surface treatment and assembly, while its portfolio of 5,654 stock-keeping units strengthens its business moat.

According to Nuvama, the long operating life of aircraft programmes supports long-term revenue visibility for qualified suppliers. It noted that Boeing's 737 programme has been running for 58 years, while the Airbus A320 programme has been in operation for 38 years.

Boeing shares gained about 4% on Thursday after a media report said two of the Asia-Pacific region's largest carriers, Singapore Airlines and Qantas Airways, are in separate talks with Boeing and Airbus to purchase dozens of wide-body aircraft.
Singapore Airlines Looks To Buy 50 Jets from Boeing And Airbus

Singapore Airlines is in early-stage discussions with Boeing and its European planemaker rival Airbus to acquire a minimum of 50 of the commercial aviation industry's largest passenger jets, Reuters reported, citing industry sources. The multi-billion-dollar acquisition is aimed at anchoring the airline's next major growth phase, which is slated to begin in the next decade.

The Singaporean flag carrier is currently evaluating the 400-seat Boeing 777X—the largest twin-engine jetliner currently available—alongside the slightly smaller Airbus A350-1000. According to sources cited by Reuters, the framework of the potential agreement could also include purchase options for dozens of additional aircraft beyond the initial 50.

EasyJet shares jump after Castlelake confirms takeover interest
sum: EasyJet shares rose as much as 12.5% on Monday after the British low-cost carrier said it would review any takeover proposal from Castlelake, while calling the timing of the US investment firm’s interest “highly opportunistic,” Reuters reported.

Castlelake said on Friday it was in the early stages of considering a possible offer for EasyJet, but said no approach had been made to the airline’s board and that there was no certainty a bid would follow.
Under UK takeover rules, Castlelake has until June 26 to either announce a firm offer or withdraw.

EasyJet said it would assess any proposal if one is made, but argued that its current share price has been depressed by the Iran war, higher fuel prices, regulatory issues and other short-term pressures.
The airline’s shares had fallen more than 22% this year before Castlelake’s interest became public. Monday’s rise lifted EasyJet’s market value to about £3.39 billion.

Castlelake is a US alternative investment firm specializing in asset-based private credit. The company says it manages about $37 billion in assets and has a dedicated aviation leasing and lending business that provides financing to airlines and aircraft owners.
The firm disclosed on Monday that it holds a 2.14% stake in EasyJet, making it one of the airline’s largest shareholders.

Airbus Shares Have Limited Upside, Analyst Sees ‘Credibility Squeeze’
sum: Airbus (ETR: AIR) is caught in a “credibility squeeze” and faces limited near-term upside despite a 15% year-to-date share price decline, according to mwb Research, which maintained its Hold rating and EUR 170.00 price target on the aerospace giant in a note on Wednesday.

Analyst Jens-Peter Rieck said Airbus is publicly maintaining its 870-delivery guidance for the year while simultaneously freezing 10% of non-industrial spending, which is a combination the firm described as “difficult to reconcile.”

The firm’s proprietary delivery tracking paints a challenging picture. Airbus delivered roughly 107 jets in the first half of the second quarter, implying a monthly run rate of 71, but by mid-May that average had slipped back to just 42 per month.
Hitting the 870-unit target would now require 97 deliveries per month for the remainder of the year, which mwb Research noted would be the strongest second half in company history.
“A formal guidance cut to around 840 is, in our view, a matter of when, not if,” the firm said.

mwb Research flagged a Reuters report that Airbus has been enforcing a 10% reduction in non-industrial spending across its Commercial Aircraft division and headquarters, running parallel to the existing LEAD cost program launched in 2024.
The signal, in the firm’s view, is that LEAD alone has proven insufficient.

Airbus Profit Falls Sharply in Q1 on Lower Deliveries, Keeps 2026 Guidance
sum: Airbus (EU:AIR) reported a significant decline in first-quarter earnings, as reduced commercial aircraft deliveries and currency pressures weighed on performance, while analysts highlighted execution and timing factors as central to the outlook.

Airbus posted revenue of €12.7 billion for the quarter, down 7% year on year and slightly below the €12.87 billion consensus estimate. Adjusted EBIT dropped to €300 million from €624 million a year earlier, while reported earnings per share declined to €0.74 from €1.01.

The commercial aircraft division was the main driver of the downturn. Deliveries fell to 114 units compared with 136 in the same period last year, pushing adjusted EBIT in the segment down to €81 million from €494 million, also impacted by less favorable hedge rates.

Free cash flow before customer financing shifted to an outflow of €2.5 billion, versus an inflow of €310 million a year earlier, reflecting lower delivery volumes and a planned inventory build linked to production ramp-up.
The Defence and Space division provided some support, with revenue rising 7% to €2.8 billion and adjusted EBIT nearly doubling to €130 million.

Chief Executive Guillaume Faury said Airbus continues to increase production "as per our plan while navigating the shortage of Pratt & Whitney engines," adding that the operating environment remains "dynamic and complex."
Analysts at Barclays said the weak first-quarter performance was largely due to timing rather than a deterioration in demand.

sum: KUALA LUMPUR, April 20 — Airbus is set to expand its defence and space footprint in Malaysia through a series of signings and key announcements scheduled to take place at the Defence Services Asia (DSA) and National Security (Natsec) Asia 2026 exhibitions this week.
Airbus president for Asia-Pacific Anand Stanley said it will be signing memoranda of understanding (MoUs) with Boustead Holdings Bhd, Airod Sdn Bhd and Global Turbine Asia Sdn Bhd (GTA).
He said the three agreements will help foster local skills and expertise through collaboration with Malaysian partners.
“It is a clear reflection of what Airbus stands for in Malaysia. Airbus is a trusted partner offering knowledge sharing and long-term cooperation across every platform we deliver.
“This indicates Airbus's support for Malaysia's National Defence Industry Policy (NDIP),” he said at Airbus’ media briefing in conjunction with the DSA and Natsec Asia 2026 exhibitions today.

Meanwhile, Zakir Hamid, head of Asia-Pacific at Airbus Defence and Space, said the collaboration with Boustead will support Malaysia in developing new knowledge and local capabilities in the space domain, while Airod and GTA will be strengthened with enhanced technical, engineering, and digital capabilities.

On Airbus’ market share, Airbus Helicopters head of Asia-Pacific Vincent Dubrule said that in the civil helicopter segment within the Asia-Pacific region (excluding India and China), Airbus leads the market with close to half of the total share — around 40 to 45 per cent.

Southwest Airlines CEO Shares Plan To Stop "Sending Passengers To Competitors" But Top Customers Are "Not Interested"
sum: Southwest Airlines passengers continue to question the carrier's updated rules and policies, from new bag fees to the "Customer of Size" rule that has left passengers humiliated. Amid the ongoing backlash, Southwest CEO Bob Jordan confirmed that the airline is exploring opening lounges to "stop sending passengers to competitors."
However, Southwest's domestic passengers, its top customers, say they are "not interested." Instead, many demand solutions to other issues, including service changes and increased costs.

During the annual Semafor World Economy summit in Washington, D.C., Southwest Airlines CEO Bob Jordan promised customers "more and more reasons" so that they could "stop sending passengers to competitors." He then confirmed that Southwest is pushing for airport lounges. The airline does not currently have its own branded lounges.

"If the customer wants something and it's meaningful, and we don't offer it, we are by default sending you to a competitor, even though you love Southwest. And we're not going to continue to do that in the future," Jordan said. "I've hinted an awful lot at lounges. We're out there looking at lounge space and things."

Back in December, Jordan told CNBC that Southwest was "actively pursuing" the possibility of opening a network of airport lounges. Two months before that, the Dallas-based airline secured a five-year lease for its first-ever VIP lounge in Terminal 2 of Daniel K. Inouye International Airport (HNL) in Honolulu, Hawaii.

The Hawaii Department of Transportation has approved a minimum construction budget of $20 million for the two-floor lounge, which is set to span over 12,200 square feet. Jordan believes "lounges would be a huge, next benefit for our customers." Unfortunately, Southwest's top customers do not share the same sentiments.

Airbus Stock Faces Rising Execution Risk Says Analyst
sum: Airbus had a challenging start to 2026, according to mwb Research, which warned in a note this week that rising operational pressures are increasing the likelihood of another revision to the company’s delivery targets.

The brokerage said its estimates point to “around 95 aircraft by mid-March 2026,” equal to 11.1 percent of the full-year goal of 870. mwb Research added that “rumours of just 6.2% as of mid-March are wrong.”
The firm noted that engine availability “is still the key bottleneck” and said the combination of supply constraints and “Middle East (ME) supply chain exposure adds further risk.”
The firm highlighted Strata’s expanded partnership to produce A320-family ailerons, a work package expected to cover about half of the manufacturer’s demand.

mwb Research wrote that the arrangement “increases the strategic relevance of ME based manufacturing,” adding that many facilities in the region “are located close to airports, which are key targets.”
Despite the elevated risk, the analysts pointed to upside from the company’s defense assets, particularly its 37.5 percent interest in MBDA.
According to mwb Research, the stake “remains below EBIT and is therefore underappreciated in the equity story,” with an estimated value of about €7 billion, or roughly 5 percent of enterprise value.

Is The Boeing C-17 Globemaster Bigger Than The Airbus A380?
sum: Commercial jet airliners are designed rather similarly to one another, with a circular or semi-circular tube, with a main deck for passenger seating, a lower deck for cargo, and a low wing mounted near the bottom of the aircraft with a dihedral angle. Airliners of the past may have had more variations, but with most modern commercial planes flying today, many differences come in smaller design choices or in size differences between different aircraft.

Military aircraft come in a wider range of shapes and sizes due to the greater variety of missions that these planes may be deployed for. Because they look so different and these types of aircraft aren't often seen side-by-side, it's not always clear how they compare to civilian airliners on size. The Boeing C-17 Globemaster III is one of the most successful military cargo planes, so how does it compare to the Airbus A380, the world's largest passenger plane?

At first glance, the Boeing C-17 Globemaster III certainly looks huge. Originally designed by McDonnell Douglas, it's a strategic transport aircraft designed to deliver outsized cargo close to battle lines, and can land on runways as short as 3,500 feet (1,067 m) or on rough/unpaved surfaces. It uses a high-mounted anhedral wing with large winglets and four Pratt & Whitney F117s, the military derivative of the PW2000 found on the Boeing 757.

The Airbus A380 entered service in 2007, 12 years after the C-17. Its basic design mimics that of other airliners, with a low-mounted dihedral wing and a conventional empennage (as opposed to the C-17's T-tail design). What makes the A380 unique is that it has two full-length passenger decks along with the cargo hold, being the only airliner to do so. It also features four engines and has the widest wingspan, the highest tail, and the highest Maximum Takeoff Weight of any airliner.

The A380 is designed to haul more passengers than any other commercial aircraft, and to be efficient while doing so. Although the A380 failed largely due to its fuel burn against newer widebodies, it was competitive against the Boeing 777 and beat the 747 on per-seat costs. The C-17 Globemaster III, in contrast, was designed for freight capacity, and although it has carried passengers before, it was developed as a cargo plane first.

Airbus stock falls on weak delivery guidance. Here's why analysts still like it
sum: - Airbus said Thursday it expects to sell 870 aircraft in 2026, below what most market watchers had expected.
- Analysts remained largely upbeat on the company, and many reiterated Buy ratings on the stock following the worse-than-expected delivery guidance, calling it a "clearing event."
- It comes as the European planemaker is facing increased competition from U.S. rival Boeing.

Airbus stock is down after its earnings painted a complicated picture: Its 2025 profits exceeded expectations, but conservative delivery guidance for 2026 and a delay in production ramp-up targets dented confidence. The stock finished Thursday's session almost 7% lower, bringing it into the red year-to-date. The stock is up more than 11% over the last 12 months, but U.S. rival Boeing is up 32% over the same period. AIR-FR BA 1Y line Boeing shares have outperformed Airbus over the past 12 months. But analysts remain largely upbeat on Airbus. Of 25 analysts covering its Paris-listed stock, 17 rate it Buy or Buy-equivalent, according to FactSet. Only one rates it Sell. Many reiterated Buy ratings on the stock following the worse-than-expected delivery guidance the company issued before the bell on Thursday, calling it a clearing event. The planemaker said it expects to sell 870 aircraft in 2026, below what most market watchers had expected. It comes as the company is trying to ramp up production of its best-selling A320 family of planes following several issues over the past few months. "Despite our cautious stance on 2026 deliveries and medium-term production rates, we believe Airbus will be a strong long-term story," said Berstein analyst Douglas Harned, who rates shares Outperform. 'An attractive entry point' J.P. Morgan analyst David Perry said that, while shares were likely to drop on the news of the delivery target, it "might be a clearing event." "If AIR can persuade investors that the new guidance is achievable this reset could provide an attractive entry point," said Perry, who rates the stock at Overweight with a price target of 240 euros. Airbus blamed one of its key suppliers, RTX -owned Pratt & Whitney, for the weak guidance.

Airbus (FY Results): solid growth but outlook disappoints
sum: Airbus’ full-year revenue rose 6% to €73.4bn. This reflected growth across all divisions, including double-digit increases in its Helicopters and Defence and Space businesses. Commercial aircraft deliveries totalled 793 (2024: 766).
Underlying operating profit rose 33% to €7.1bn (£6.9bn expected), with the uplift driven by a sharp return to profitability in the Defence & Space division.
Free cash flow improved from €4.5bn to €4.6bn. The net cash position rose from €11.8bn to €12.2bn.
In 2026, Airbus expects to deliver around 870 commercial aircraft (907 expected). Underlying operating profits and free cash flow are expected to land at around €7.5bn and €4.5bn respectively.
A dividend of €3.20 per share was announced, up 7% when including last year’s special dividend.

Airbus delivered a solid performance in 2025, with profits landing ahead of expectations thanks to a strong performance in the Defence & Space division. But the outlook for 2026 was worse than expected across the board. Alongside delays from one of its engine suppliers, the longer-term production ramp-up has been cut back slightly, causing the shares to fall on the day.

At its core, Airbus builds aircraft using thousands of parts from companies worldwide. Market dynamics are very favourable given it’s dominated by just two companies, with the split standing at roughly 60/40 in Airbus’ favour. Meanwhile, high barriers to entry help to keep outside competition at bay.

Fewer Planes, Same Profit: How Airbus Is Protecting Its Billions Despite The A320 Stumble
sum: With the recent issues affecting A320 aircraft around the world, resulting in operational disruptions as carriers have had to ground the affected aircraft to remedy the issue, Airbus has decided to slash its target for commercial aircraft deliveries for this year.

However, the manufacturer has indicated that the financial performance for the year remains unchanged. While the expected number of aircraft deliveries has been reduced by 30, the question remains: how is Airbus ensuring its bottom line is not affected?

Airbus has decided to reduce the number of targeted commercial aircraft deliveries to 790 aircraft this year. According to reports from The National, this is down 30 aircraft from the originally intended 820 deliveries in 2025. The reason for this decrease in the delivery target is due to the issues faced by the Airbus A320 family aircraft recently. These included quality problems faced by Spanish supplier Sofitec Aero, which affected some of the aircraft's fuselage panels.

This resulted in over 600 aircraft having to be inspected. Elsewhere, a software glitch affected around half the global fleet. Reports from The National indicate that, of the 628 aircraft that had to have their fuselage panels inspected, 168 examples are currently in commercial service. Despite these issues forcing the manufacturer to reduce its delivery forecast for the remainder of the year, Airbus specifies that its 2025 financial guidance will remain unchanged:
"The Company still targets an EBIT Adjusted of around €7.0 billion and Free Cash Flow before Customer Financing of around €4.5 billion."

The first issue the A320 faced was a software glitch, which prompted an Airworthiness Directive and Airbus to ground over 6,000 aircraft. This represented around half of the narrowbody family's global fleet. While a fix was made available quickly by rolling back the affected aircraft to the previous version of the software, it still caused operational disruptions to airlines around the world, resulting in flight delays and cancellations.
While some carriers experienced relatively short disruptions, those with a large number of A320 family aircraft in their fleets faced more complex problems.

sum: Airbus's share price dropped as much as 10% on Monday morning after the planemaker found an issue with some components for its best-selling A320 aircraft.
In a statement, Airbus said a "supplier quality issue" affected "a limited number of A320 metal panels."
Airbus didn't disclose exactly how many planes were potentially affected.

"As it always does when faced with quality issues in its supply chain, Airbus is taking a conservative approach and is inspecting all aircraft potentially impacted — knowing that only a portion of them will need further action to be taken," the statement continued.
"The source of the issue has been identified, contained, and all newly produced panels conform to all requirements."
Airbus's share price opened at 201.15 euros and fell as low as 183 euros after Reuters first reported on the issue.
However, it has pared some of the losses, and the stock was down 6.5% as of 8:10 a.m. ET.
